Let's assume (JUST ASSUME) that Anarch Revolt needs fixing. Let's not
enter the "does it need fixing or not" debate. How would it be best
fixed?

There have been a few suggestions of late. Take your pick and say your
piece. Might even be worth doing a vote...

Solution No 1
Change the damage timing. Make the damage payable in the Discard
phase, giving almost a turn of grace to sort it, and also means the
"Revolter" has to pay in the same turn.

Solution No 2
Stop them stacking. Make it Unique or Make it like Army of Rats (i.e.
max of 1 pool damage regardless of numbers in play).

Solution No 3
Make them easier to get rid of. E.g. Like National Guard Support. OR
change the vote to remove one Anarch Revolt to "call a referendum to
remove all Anarch Revolts from play".

Solution No 4
Give an "easy out" solution. E.g. Make it so if you control a ready
Anarch you are immune to the pool damage.

Solution No 5
Change the terms. Change it from a vote to remove the revolts to a
straight action to remove the revolt (maybe with some extra kick -
e.g. "Any vampire with a capacity above 5 may take an Action to remove
this Anarch Revolt from play", or maybe add a blood cost).

Solution No 6
Get rid of it! Ban the card from Tournaments

I think these are the main, sensible ones.

Thoughts?

Dave

P.S. My favourite solution is in no. 3 - one vote to kill ALL Anarch
Revolts in play.

The number of different ways terms can be set isn't a criterion for
determining if a the referendum can be called again after Delaying
Tactics.

Even if every Anarch Revolt had the same referendum (e.g. "burn all
Anarch Revolts in play") with no choices to be made, they'd still be
different actions. So after DT, the acting minion couldn't call any
referendum this turn (per the usual rules on political actions, not
because of any special effect of DT), but other vampires would be
free to call the referendum given on other Anarch Revolts in play;

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
colind...@aol.com (Colin Goodman) wrote in message news:<20030904065303...@mb-m12.aol.com>...

> Maybe I missed something, but whats wrong with Anarch Revolt that you feel it
> needs changing?

Well, a lot of folks feel that Anarch Revolt is simply too disruptive
to play and too easy to use. Anarch Revolt decks (i.e. decks that
generally put 1 or 2 Anarch Revolts into play every turn)tend to
completely destroy any game they are in. And while Anarch Revolt decks
tend to lose more often than not (and tend to make some random player
across the table win, just by luck), people keep playing them as there
is little disincentive to do so (other than losing). Most other deck
strategies that don't win manage to do so without completely
demolishing the table. Anarch Revolt decks, however, simply make
*everyone* suck, and tend to end games very quickly and randomly.

Many people think than Anarch Revolt should have been (or be) adjusted
to make it less attractive to play--perhaps changing when the damage
happens to the end of the turn rather than the beginning (so the guy
playing it takes the damage before anyone else); or making it cost a
pool to put into play; or making it cost X pool, where X is the number
of Anarch Revolts already in play. Something to make people consider
building decks out of them. As it currently stand, Anarch Revolt seems
viable enough to justify making a deck around them, which, generally
speaking, they aren't, and just make you lose. But if the card had
some higher cost, people would probably realize this sooner than
later.

-Peter

Actually, what I'm saying is that irresponsible bleed DOES upset table
balance, sometimes as much as an AR deck. A common complaint about
the game is that you can't play a tournament deck without bounce, and
while that is not necessarily true, it's an exaggeration with some
basis in fact. I have been in tournament rounds in which the
irresonsible bleeder turned the game into a test of who was out of
bounce. So no, the bleeder is not just helping their prey win. S/he
might in fact be helping their grand-predator win, or even their
predator. If you want to look straight at the effects, irresponsible
bleed is more of an unbalancing factor than ARs partially because of
the fact that revolts do hit everyone in a consistent and predictable
manner. If you are unable or unwilling to block a bleed there are
exactly four cards that allow you to send it somewhere else, combined
with a small smattering of cards that allow you to reduce the amount
of that bleed. Compare that to the number of cards and strategies
that allow you to gain pool. I would never call a deck a losing deck
because it had no bounce, as long as it had some hope of dealing with
stealth-bleed that maybe just didn't pan out. I WOULD call a deck a
losing deck if it has no pool gain. Anarch Revolt does nothing on its
own but make this factor more urgent for everyone equally. I guess
what I'm saying is that I don't buy the "random king-maker" factor as
much, because I think irresponsible bleed is a worse random
king-maker.

have seen AR decks played by very good players that sweep or at least
game-win nearly every time they're played. The card by itself is not
random. It's just that it creates a much larger set of
partially-controllable factors than most people are able to handle.
Essentially it condenses the problems of table-management into a much
smaller timespace while turning the table against you, making it
harder to create deals. Which is why it is not a strategy for the
faint of heart. (I'll go ahead and give credit where credit is due.
The most consistent winning with AR decks I personally have seen was
done by Stu Pieloch, Prince of Portland, my former playgroup.)

In essence, a bad AR deck does what many bad decks do - it hurts its
prey with no thought to what's happening to the rest of the table.
The essence of V:TES is this - Forward motion wins a point, table
management wins the game.

And now I suppose I will toss in my answer to the hypothetical
question that started all this. Even if Anarch Revolt is not broken,
could it be improved by "fixing?" I generally don't assume that
things are fine as is, so I'm willing to look at this possibility.

First of all, I don't think we need to add a mechanic to limit the
number of Revolts in play. Doing so renders it useless as a
game-winning strategy, which would utterly marginalize the card. (We
already have a rarely-used card like that. It's called Antediluvian
Awakening.) Also, whereas AA has a cancel cost that many are
unwilling to pay, anyone with spare actions will call a vote to get
rid of an AR. Limiting the number in play makes it all the more
useless because its cancel cost is minimal. Because of this, I also
think that making it not stack (like Army of Rats) would marginalize
the card as well. People frequently have spare minions with animalism
to put Rats into play, but who would be willing to spare the master
phase action for no more than one per turn when, again, the card is so
fragile? Because the card is so fragile, I also think the last thing
that needs to be done is make it more fragile. Getting rid of all
Revolts in play with a single vote is definitely unnecessary
considering the amount of table cooperation they normally engender.

So then we get to the ideas of making it hurt the person who played it
a little more. Either making it cost a pool or perhaps take effect
during the discard phase (thus costing the owner and allowing his/her
prey a chance to get rid of it before being affected). This has more
of an Army of Rats feel, and I think it could still be playable. The
difficulty with this is it is largely unprecedented. Things happen
during untap in V:TES, they don't happen during discard.

Most of all, though, I get the impression that you, Peter, just don't
like seeing quite so many at a time. I can understand that, so I
think I go with the idea of making it a Trifle. Yes, I know people
think this actually powers it up, but it builds in a desired detriment
while keeping it very playable. Combine it with a timing change if
you want. Any more than that and it becomes wallpaper.

And as to the question of what it would hurt to make it
cost-prohibitive or even to eliminate entirely? That one I can
definitely answer. Anarch Revolt is about the only card that can
motivate some wall decks to move forward. Harbingers/Slaughterhouse
decks HATE Anarch Revolt because it makes them move before they want
to. If your prey is an intercept-heavy Harbingers deck that just
wants to sit there and block everything your minions do until everyone
is out of cards, how else can you damage their pool? You would need
some sort of master card that could hurt them. And you'd probably
need a stack of several of them.

So yes, I think Anarch Revolt needs to be in the game (and kept
effective) because it can be one of the few ways to break a wall. So
look at it this way - the more Anarch Revolt gets hurt, the more
likely I am to play Brinksmanship. :)

Nah. Never protect your Anarch Revolts. Other people voting them down
guarantees that your prey loses far more pool to them than you do.

You don't spend much pool, 'cause you only bring out one vampire and a
few locations, and you lose less pool to the revolts than every one

Minion Tap/Golconda every other turn. That's old school; I've been

Dep, etc., you should include some Secure Havens...you only have one
vampire out, so that's total coverage. Votes can be the toughest
offense to deal with. Either plan to weather them or include a few
Dread Gaze/DTs, depending on your metagame.

Bleeding is unnecessary. Let AR and other players do the damage for
you, then clean up with votes.

Yes, Anson is a prince. I recommend a few Obfuscate masters in the
deck so you can Forgotten Labrynth with him. Awe and/or BO will pass
your votes when you need to.

One final note: your library should be 60 cards, or even fewer if
local rules allow. You'll never see its bottom.

The "or it would always win" argument is simply not correct.

Not everyone chooses decks based solely on what deck they
think is the strongest. A lot of people seem to get bored
with playing the same deck all the time, or playing the
"obvious" decks all the time, and play various less-strong
concepts just for the sake of variety and their own (or
others') entertainment. Even in tournaments.

Besides that, an overpowered card doesn't have to result
in its deck always winning. It just increases the chances
of its deck winning.

Beyond this, an unbalanced card isn't *necessarily* one
that makes its player win a lot. It can have too large an
effect for its cost, even if the effect isn't always going
to be useful in making its player win. This is where I
think Anarch Revolt fits: it causes (in a 5-player game) 5
pool loss per time around the table, for the cost of 0
pool and 1 master phase action. Conservative Agitation,
by comparison, requires an unblocked action, passing a vote,
and using a card each time you want to get the effect (and
is still a strong card). Slave Auction can gain you 4
pool, but costs 6 master phase actions to do so (and takes
6 times around the table too).

Anarch Revolt not only speeds attrition up, it makes many types of
decks completely unplayable due to its speed and inevitability of the
outcome. Unless you have immediate ways to bloat and bloat heavily,
you will be destroyed in short order. The only other option is to
eliminate the AR players means of bloating. In the JOL tournament, I
took my Assamites upstream against Wouter's Anarch Revolt deck to
deprive him of any chance to bloat. It was my only way to survive. Due
to some freaky table mechanics, I was able to get 1 VP, but that
wouldn't have happened otherwise.

The main reason I think we don't see more Anarch Revolt decks making
the rounds is peer pressure. I think the sentiment that Anarch Revolt
is "cheese" is nearly universal. It's "cheese" because none of the
three major strategies (bleed, politics or combat) are being utilized.
There are players who don't consider the cheese factor a taboo against
playing it, and that's just fine. But most others don't want to have a
local stigma attached to them for playing decks that "require no
skill" to play, even though decision-making for the AR player is
paramount. If this peer pressure weren't in place, I think we'd see
many more Anarch Revolt decks played because they can win and win big.

Most VTES players want to have *FUN* when playing and AR really isn't
fun for most people. In casual play, there is almost no chance to set
up some funky combo deck or bizarre Anarch or Ally strategy. In
tournaments, Anarch Revolt often rears its ugly head and that can
contribute to the casual player's disgust with the tournament
environment. If White Wolf is promoting tournaments as a marketing
tool, they'd better hope players are enjoying themselves while they
participate. The VTES player base isn't nearly as cutthroat as that of
other CCGs, and I think that to keep things growing we shouldn't fall
into the trap of going for hyper-competitiveness.

Expand on this in a way. It's much harder to determine problem cards in
multiplayer CCGs. Sure, someone can make the "if everyone has to gang up to
stop it, then it's broken" argument except that this argument rarely has
results to support it since good players do gang up to stop it whereas with
two-player CCGs (accurate) results (from competent players) are an excellent
source for supporting arguments.

Even in tournament play, social factors affect the strength of decks. Peer
pressure not to play distasteful decks often works on a local basis which is
unfortunate. Unfortunate in that problem cards/strategies are often not
sufficiently examined as too many regions peer pressure out decks they find
distasteful without necessarily realizing it. This, in turn, means less
rigorous analysis of the game and less complaint about what's truly wrong with
it when played on the most competitive level and more complaint about what's
wrong in regional metagames.

Certainly, it's the point of individual card text to provide variety to a CCG.
However, if only a single card (unlikely) or a tiny fraction of the cards
(probable) cause a game to play completely differently such that one is playing
a "different" game even if the game isn't a stronger one, then it's the case
that those cards are badly designed.

Anarch Revolt has some positive features. It produces viable and distinctive
archetypes. The problem is that it can also eliminate the viability of a
greater number of archetypes. This goes to the issue of fun in CCGing (taking
a cue from Mike Nudd's post). Not every deck has to be competitive; there are
always going to be stronger and weaker decks; but, it's more fun to have more
options of viable decks.

It's also more fun to have quality interaction and AR's strength comes from how
hard it is to interact with.

AR is not the only antifun culprit. Weenie decks all but guarantee killing one
player only being balanced by burning out too fast too often to guarantee
victory. The ease of bleeding heavily forces a major metagame presence of
bleed bounce. And, so on*. Maybe it's not possible to rein all of the problem
areas in a CCG in to produce a balanced environment, but it's worth constantly
considering what's problematic in a CCG in case a little pain - errata,
banning, rules change - can result in a greater benefit.

* Decks running at different speeds is often at the heart of complaints how
something isn't fun. Some variation of speed is likely necessary. Wide
variations means something isn't going to be fun to play.

be fun, but that's supposed to derive from people's love of
competition, strategy & tactics.) If a strategy is more bizarre than
effective, then it will lose more often than not. Sometimes, the
simplest strategies and tactics are the best. That's not to say that
bizarre strategies cannot win. It's just that they have to eventually
boil down to removing the prey's pool faster than their own pool is
being removed.

very social, and players know better than to keep playing the same deck
repetitively if it's going to cause a lot of grief amongst their friends.
Secondly, most of our players are extremely inventive, and can pull new and
competitive decks out which are likely to do well (not considering of course
the likely impact of stacked AR). Thirdly, many of our players rely on the
element of surprise, and they know damn well that if they keep playing the
same deck then people will build decks not to win, but to specifically
outlive it or kill it off, and so they pre-empt this from happening by
switching decks.

next

I would have to disagree. A potence rush deck is really only going to affect
it's prey and it's predator (although it has the potential to cross-table if
necessary). If you're sitting next to a *good* potence rush deck, then you
may have your work cut out for you, but it's not an insurmoutnable problem.

If you're playing a competitive combat deck of your own, then you should be
able to hold your ground, or at least take them with you as Potence combat
usually lacks a lot of prevention. If you want to stay out of combat then
just packing a few S:CEs isn't going to cut it, so pack Obedience,
prevention, or cards that end combat like Purchase Pact or Elysium: the
Arboretum. Or at least pack maneuvers to avoid the IGs. If you're voting
then Banish the rushing vampires, and if you're bloating, then just keep
bringing out new vampires. Don't do stupid things like blocking the Potence
vampires when you don't need to. If the Potence deck is getting the upper
hand, then work with the other players on the table to shut it down. If he's
blocking you, then just stealth past or play crazy stuff like Kiss of Ra.
There are a myriad of ways of dealing with this kind of problem, and that's
not even considering hand jam on the part of the Potence player, who may not
be able to draw the rush cards or IG cards he needs in any case. If you
can't do *anything* except take it like a bitch then I'm afraid you should
really build yourself a better deck... :)

With a good stacked AR deck it's a completely different problem. You've got
two options:

a) bloat like a bastard to outlive every other deck on the table
b) use all your actions to kill the ARs, which *only* works if there enough
allied votes on the table

This means that playing any other deck or strategy is pretty much a waste of
time, and if you come to the table without being able to do a) or b) you're
dead in the water, regardless of where you sit on the table. This strikes me
as being a very unfair, unenjoyable situation.

potence rush has on the game. Maybe Immortal Grapple, but IG is too important

It depends. I'd point out to you that the decks I play are not completely
due to personal playing style. They're also a response to local metagame,
as everyone's should be. If you play where there's a lot of combat decks,
especially potence combat decks, then it's fairly reasonable to rely on cards
that neutralize it. However, I've noticed that potence rush combat is
extremely hard to prepare for in places that have a lot more sneaky,
stealthy decks that are geared towards screwing with opponents by getting
actions past blockers somehow. As I said in another post, you weaken
yourself far too much against the rest of the field by trying to cover
this one single type of deck. That's what irritates me about it.
There's nothing else in the game I can think of that doesn't get covered
by fairly standard "good cards" that you'd be well-advised to use anyway if
you can spare the deckspace for them. Most gadget decks are covered by
sufficient intercept. Anything that packs too much stealth to be
regularly stopped by a fair amount of intercept is too simple to be very
powerful. The exception is bleed - which you bounce or at least try to make
them choke on their stealth. Only trying to cover potence rush combat with
IG and maneuvers (basically Brujah rush) makes you pack things you wouldn't
need against anything else.

It's not that rush combat is unbalanced. If you play where combat abounds,
it's certainly going to run into combat decks that will take it out. It's
just where combat *isn't* that common that it seems to have this effect
that leaves people having to decide whether to prepare for it or for
everything else. And if such rush combat decks actually usually won in
places like that because they had a metagame advantage, I wouldn't mind so
much. Then it would just be a sign that everyone else needed to adjust
what they were doing. But usually, it seems like they just crush their
neighbors a lot more than they actually win games.

you to use large enough vampires to win the cap comparison. Thus, it's
really not worth doing with even mid-caps, since they become dead weight
against large combat vampires. Fortitude is better but to be useful, you
have usually have to take up more deckspace with it than, say, S:CE.

against so many other common decks that I've given up bothering with it
myself.

in practice. I mean, if you want to suggest dreamland solutions, you
could propose to slap Brainwashes down on all his vampires but it wouldn't

someone's "answer" to a problem don't seem very realistic. Even I can
come up with better answers myself than Banish and bloat.

likely to win after you've solved the rush combat deck problem is another

those vampires out, then he's got vote lock. Frankly, there are decks that
are *much* better geared to take advantage of vote lock than any AR deck I've
ever seen.

What it usually takes is just simple cooperation between the other players.
Given that, I've never noticed that it's hard at all to stop an AR deck.
The issue is really about who took what collateral damage as it's being
stopped. That's a legitimate complaint about the deck. But I'd rather see
an AR deck than potence rush any day.

> > > Perhaps most importantly, because facing stacked AR is so unenjoyable,
> > > it's going to completely put off any new players that make
> > > an effort to come along to an event for the first time.

> > It really shouldn't. I think you just have to explain the situation

>
> "Huh this is my first time and someone cross-table killed me at random

> game sucks."

If that's happening a lot, then you guys aren't doing a good job of stopping
the ARs. And YES! Once in a while you get cross-table killed at random in
this game. AR decks are hardly the only thing guilty of that in this game.
Just more guilty than most.

Fred

Not to intrude too much in this discussion, especially as it seems to have
gotten far away from AR though I don't feel like changing the subject line, but
there is a difference between voting, bleeding, and fighting. The defenses for
each of the first two are narrower, thus easier to implement. General ways to
stop voting - intercept, more votes, DT. Bleed decks have a bit more
variation, but bounce, reduction, intercept wall will have an effect on all of
them. With combat, once you get past the defense of never entering combat
which you often don't have control over, the defenses against particular brands
of combat will vary tremendously.

I think this goes to the heart of Fred's complaint. If not, it goes to the
heart of my complaint about combat fairness. Combat lends itself to producing
more unfair matchups than voting and bleeding because reasonable defenses
against an open metagame either require restricting viable deck archetypes or
require devoting too much space to defense. Put another way, in a tournament
situation, I don't play games where I think "my predator's a bleed deck, I'm
screwed". (Though, the problem of weenie decks is the first prey *is* screwed
in almost every game, but the problem of weenie decks is worthy of its own
complaints.) But, it's quite possible to think "my predator's combat trumps my
combat, I'm screwed". Could be IG, could be Protean, could be Entombment,
anti-dodge, steal blood, unpreventable damage, etc., and there's even the
possibility that an opponent's lack of combat can screw you by making bunches
of cards in your deck dead draws. There's an element of turning games into
crap shoots. I got tired of craps before I got out of high school.

>
> It sounds very much like you're chasing your own tail - the same argument

Hardly. I've had this argument with others, so I don't really intend to
spend time with it again. But what it boils down to is that rush combat
decks that torporize or burn vampires basically work differently than
other decks, bleed decks, votes decks, or whatever that try to work on
someone's pool directly. The rush decks that put out two or three combat
monsters destroy pool by preventing you from ever keeping a vampire on
the board. If you can't keep a vampire on the board, you can't do anything
at all. But, ironically, the fastest way to oust yourself with a combat
neighbor is to put vampires out for them to destroy. If you just let them
bleed you, they take forever. I've seen people successfully resist
being ousted by a rush predator when the predator tipped off what his deck
was (by rushing his predator). Then, they influence everyone to within
four transfers of bringing them all up - but not quite. Then, they sit
there and watch the predator rush everyone else at the table trying to
keep it stable and eventually burning himself out doing that.

That's a totally stupid way to have to defend yourself, but in a metagame
where it's not worth packing a lot of combat defense, that's what you have
to do.

> A very focused
> combat deck is going to get past most opponents, except for those that pack
> anti-combat and/or combat of their own, or alternative ways of shutting the
> opposing vampires down.

Unfortunately, that's a generalized statement that's not very accurate when
you get to looking at the details. "Packing anti-combat" is one thing.
Packing enough anti-combat cards to save you against a rush deck is so
different that it's usually not worth doing. You can kind of do it if
you happen to be playing a fortitude clan or (as you suggested), large
dominate vampires that can obedience. But there's a lot of different
decks archetypes for which trying to throw in enough to stop a rush/potence/
celerity deck is far more card intensive than what you have to do against
95% of the combat you're usually going to see. It's not worth it.

> Do you
> actually have a point, because it sounds like you just keep whinging about
> the fact that you can't build decks to stand up to heavy combat...?

I have a point. You just keep ignoring it and proceed to respond to to a
different point I've never tried to make. It's not about being unable to cope
with these kinds of decks. It's about it not being worthwhile to do so -
and then when you do play against them, they unbalance tables a lot more than
they win games.

> > > In contrast slapping down large multiples of AR affects *every* player

> > > on the table, and to such a degree that the game ends randomly in only
> > > a small number of turns so that there is barely enough time to react.
> >
> > But only some of the time. And often enough, I feel that when it happens
> > it's mainly because the opponents of the AR deck played poorly.
>
> But that 'some of the time' is enough. I'm not worried about seeing 1 or 2
> ARs on the table as there is obviously plenty of opportunity to get rid of
> them, and yes, tough s*** for those players who don't make an effort to get
> rid of them, get rid of the controller's vampires, or bloat up to counter
> the pool loss (which isn't that bad, and no different really from taking a
> bleed each turn). What I'm talking about is when you get say 5 or more on
> the table mid- to end-game from nowhere (using multiple master actions).

So, I ask you, how do get "five or more on the table" without there only
being one or two on the table at some point. Most you can ever put out on
a turn is three. That's a whole turn to get rid of the ones that are out
there.

> *Most* decks simply won't have enough time to turn against the AR controller
> before they are ousted, and the offending deck only needs to fend the table
> off for 2 or 3 turns before it's all over.

Bleh. If it gets to that point, people haven't cooperated to do what they
have to do. Or the AR players has been tremendously lucky. How do you get
Anson (or alternately pass a Rumors of Gehenna) AND the Parthenon out
AND start drawing and dumping three ARs a turn AND draw enough of the
right cards to effectively frustrate votes before ALL of your opponents
get enough stuff out to vote the ARs off the table? It normally can't
be done unless people pass up a significant number of chances to get rid
of an AR. And almost any game I've seen where ARs have gotten out of hand,
that's exactly what happened.

I understand the temptation to let one or two go and to act in self-
interest. Sometimes, it turns out to the right thing to do. But if
you wind back the sort of game you're talking about, I guarantee you almost
all of them will involve a fair number of times someone chose to bleed (not
just to get the Edge in friendly hands) or act to build up his position
or something that wasn't necessary to stopping the ARs.

> In fact, IMHO the best use of
> Anarch Revolt does seem to be to play it late to take people by surprise.
> This is unequivocally bad.

Sorry, I still disagree. Again, you can't "suddenly" plop down five ARs.
If you play them late, what were you doing up until then? You can't
expect to be an AR deck if you don't have a lot of AR cards and support
for them. And you're not going to be good at anything else if you've
got a bunch of AR cards in your deck and clogging up your hand. So you're
not going to be able to do much about putting your prey in position to be
ousted (let alone line the table up to fall right) such that suddenly
dumping five ARs makes for easy win. If this is how people in your area
are winning with Anarch Revolts, the rest of you are doing something wrong.

Anyway, I'd say it's kind of self-contradictory to say ARs make the game
end too fast...but they're not played until the mid-game or end game.
It sounds like people are half ousting themselves and then bitching because
an AR deck suddenly pushes them over the top.

> Large amounts of ARs end the game far
> too quickly, and to me this runs contrary to what the metagame is supposed
> to be all about. Nothing you have said so far addresses this.

I have. I'm don't see how you can conclude that the metagame is "supposed"
to be about anything. In that sense, all AR decks do is change the nature
of a game to be much faster than a lot of people plan for - which means
essentially that they LOST the metagame by creating a slow-moving deck.
That's certainly fair enough, in my humble opinion. The only actual
*problem* here is when AR decks destabilize the table and create ousts which
do not help the AR player and randomly help someone else - which, as it
said, is already a far worse property of a rush combat deck.

Fred
